The President doesn’t believe he is subject to constraints, but the Constitution and the law require Congressional approval for any broad-based military action.
 
Today’s vote is the first vote in holding the President accountable to those constraints and doing our duty under the Constitution, which says clearly that only Congress can declare war.
 
The President has taken broad military action in Iran, taking out government leaders, bombing key military targets, and trying to destroy Iran’s ballistic missile arsenal.
 
While deterring dangerous regimes from developing nuclear weapons is a critical mission, this effort has gone far beyond key strikes on timely, urgent targets.
 
That is why the President must come to Congress if he wants broad military authority.
 
Under the Constitution and the War Powers Resolution, Congress has the power to declare war, while the President, as Commander in Chief, may only use military force without prior congressional approval to repel sudden attacks and respond to clear imminent threats. 
 
Americans want to know the plan. With our economy in turbulence and working people wanting us to focus on their immediate economic needs and combatting inflation, it is hard to argue that an expensive, risky, and disruptive military venture in the Middle East is the right action to take now.
 
Today’s vote is important for reaffirming our belief that any broad military engagement that risks loss of life and treasure must be approved by Congress.
 
Instead, we should focus on tougher sanctions and a vigorous inspection regime to stop Iran from getting nuclear weapons.
 
The American people deserve to know where Congress stands. The Constitution puts constraints on the President. My colleagues on the other side of aisle should help rein in the President when he continues to ignore those constitutional constraints, including on tariffs, free speech, voting rights and now war powers. They should not just give the President a free hand.

My statement on the House passage of my bill to end the Democrat shutdown and fully fund Homeland Security:

The Constitution places the safety and security of the American people at the center of the federal government’s responsibilities. It is a duty I don’t take lightly. Amidst rising global tensions and natural disaster possibilities, jeopardizing security operations and emergency preparedness is the last thing anyone should be doing. Yet, Democrats have kept the Department of Homeland Security shuttered for weeks – and again voted to keep it that way.

They are actively choosing to deny resources to the very people responsible for protecting the American homeland. Cybersecurity operations are at limited capacity, as adversaries like Iran, Russia, and China seek to exploit infrastructure vulnerabilities. Training for first responders has been canceled. FEMA grants – utilized by state and local entities to ensure safety and combat terrorism – can’t be accessed. TSA officers are being forced to work through the shutdown while missing paychecks. Coast Guard men and women, including those in harm’s way in Bahrain, are completing missions without full resources behind them. Even security preparations to keep attendees safe at the America 250 celebrations, the FIFA World Cup, the LA2028 Olympics, and more face disruptions. These impacts are not political or hyperbole. They are the direct cost of Democrats’ decision to play politics with the safeguards of this country.

My priority is serving and protecting Oklahomans and all Americans, which is why I voted again today to pass full-year DHS funding. No selective resourcing – full operational funding for the Department of Homeland Security and the personnel who stand watch over this nation every day. Despite bipartisan majorities in both chambers, a small minority of Democrats continue to hold this funding hostage. However, let me be clear: shielding the homeland should never be treated as a political bargaining chip.

We in Congress can debate the merits of the War Powers Act, but the hard reality is that the President has committed U.S. troops to active engagement in combat with an enemy that has targeted and killed Americans for decades. We have lost six soldiers in this fight with the potential for more casualties. What our troops need now is for our Congress, and this country, to know that they are supported. It is for this reason that I oppose Senator Kaine’s War Powers Resolution—based on the practical implications of its passage.

As written, it requires removal of troops from hostilities, leaving no room for operations that have already started to reach an even partially successful conclusion to degrade Iran’s nuclear capabilities. As Iran attacks everything it can, from military bases to embassies to civilian targets, we cannot tie our military’s hands or abruptly leave our allies and partners to fight on their own.

There is no question that the President should have sought authorization from Congress before striking Iran on this scale, likewise bringing in our allies ahead of time as they now are equally in danger. However, the abrupt cessation of all offensive operations would not leave any Americans—soldiers, diplomats, or civilians—in the Middle East in a safer position.

The President acknowledged in his notification to Congress that no one knows the full scope and duration of military operations that may be necessary. It then becomes the duty of Congress to define the scope of this conflict, requiring the President to fully and transparently make his case for this action. We should begin drafting and debating an authorization for the use of military force, critically examining requests for supplemental funding, as well as conduct rigorous oversight hearings, so the American people know the limits and objectives of this military operation.

My focus is on the safety of America’s armed forces and the American civilians who are on the ground in the Middle East. At this point, we have little choice but to continue the military operation to degrade and destroy Iran’s capability for nuclear weapons. That will not happen without support for our U.S. military.

P000597.text:
RT by @chelliepingree: 🚨 FARM BILL POWER GRAB

The 2026 Farm Bill quietly slipped in three sections that could shield pesticide companies from lawsuits, block states from regulating chemicals, and weaken water protections nationwide.

Rep. Chellie Pingree just introduced an amendment to delete them entirely.

Here’s the plain-English breakdown everyone should understand 👇

1. Lawsuit Shield for Pesticide Companies (Section 10205)

If this stays in the bill, chemical companies could avoid liability even if new evidence shows their product causes cancer or neurological damage. As long as the pesticide followed the label approved under Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA), victims may lose the ability to sue.

Why this matters:

Bayer has already paid about $11 billion to settle lawsuits over the herbicide Glyphosate linked to non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma. More than 165,000 claims have been filed against Bayer tied to the product Roundup herbicide.

If Section 10205 passes, future cases like those could be blocked.

Pingree’s amendment removes that shield.

2. States Lose Power Over Pesticide Rules (Section 10206)

Right now states and local governments can create stricter pesticide protections than the federal government.

That includes things like bans on spraying near schools or buffer zones around homes and waterways.

Section 10206 would override those rules nationwide.

That reverses precedent set by the Supreme Court case
Wisconsin Public Intervenor v. Mortier, which affirmed that local governments can regulate pesticides.

Seven states currently allow local pesticide control.
Those protections could disappear overnight.

3. Weakened Water & Wildlife Protections (Section 10207)

This provision would exempt pesticides from additional review under major environmental laws including the Clean Water Act and the Endangered Species Act.

In practice that means pesticides approved by EPA could enter rivers, streams, and habitats without additional permits or environmental review.

Government monitoring has already detected pesticide residues in most U.S. waterways, raising concerns about runoff impacts on fish, wildlife, and drinking water.

Why This Fight Is Exploding

Critics argue the provisions protect chemical manufacturers, override state authority, and weaken environmental oversight.

Supporters claim the sections reduce litigation risk, simplify national pesticide regulation, and protect agricultural production.

Pingree’s amendment simply removes the three sections entirely, restoring the existing regulatory framework.

What Happens Next

The bill is still in markup inside the House Agriculture Committee.

That means these provisions can still be removed before the Farm Bill moves forward.

This fight will determine who controls pesticide rules in America — communities or chemical companies.

Key Takeaways

The Farm Bill includes three provisions that could shield pesticide companies from lawsuits.

They could also strip states and towns of authority to regulate pesticide use locally.

Environmental protections tied to waterways and wildlife could be weakened.

The Pingree amendment would remove those provisions entirely and restore current law. @amtoxicology @chelliepingree

B001295.text: I met with the Illinois Farm Bureau’s new president, Philip Nelson, to talk about the recent Farm Bill negotiations and the importance of year-round E15 biofuels. Serving on the House Committee on Agriculture allows me to bring these priorities directly to Congress as we continue to work to pass a Farm Bill that gives farmers across Southern Illinois the certainty they deserve, now that it has made its way out of the House Agriculture Committee.

Things got a little heated in the House Agriculture Committee this week, where we were marking up the now-approved 2026 Farm Bill. The final package – which secures much needed funding for Southern Illinois’ farmers, ensures access to credit, and expands rural broadband – also includes my SOLAR Act legislation. It protects farmers’ rights to determine what happens on their land, but it stops taxpayer dollars from being used to incentivize taking prime farmland out of production for the purpose of installing massive solar panel projects. Some of my Democrat colleagues tried to remove my language from the bill, and I wasn’t happy about it. They weren’t successful.

D000624.text:
President Trump’s announcement today that he plans to replace Secretary Kristi Noem by the end of the month is long overdue. For months, I’ve called on the administration to remove her from her position since her leadership put politics ahead of the safety, rights, and trust of the American people. 

Secretary Noem’s tenure at the Department of Homeland Security was deeply troubling and marked by repeated controversies—from questions about her department’s oversight, to her decisions to spend federal dollars for personal gain. Most concerning of all, two Americans were shot and killed in Minnesota by immigration enforcement agents under her command this year. It is clear she was not fit to lead an agency with such immense responsibility. 

But replacing one official does not fix the deeper problems. I hope the new leadership of the Department of Homeland Security will implement strong reforms that rein in ICE agents and that they understand the serious responsibility of this agency. The American people deserve leadership at DHS that respects the law, protects civil liberties, and is held accountable.

Instead of Alaska traveling 5,000 miles to Washington, we brought the Senate to Alaska.

Last week, as chairman of the @SenateCommerce Subcommittee overseeing the Coast Guard, I chaired a hearing at UAA with experts on Arctic security and the critical role Alaska plays in national defense, highlighting investments in the Port of Nome, reactivating Adak Naval Air Station, and the largest investment in @USCG history, which includes 16 new icebreakers, with some being home-ported in Alaska—where the ice is.

As incursions by America's adversaries continue into Alaska's ADIZ/EEZ, this military buildup—literally billions of dollars in historic investments—must continue.

I was out running on the Mall again this morning before I head back home for the Iditarod weekend. Once again, I ran into some great young men and women serving in the National Guard—the same unit from Mississippi I bumped into a few weeks ago!

@SenatorWicker and @SenHydeSmith, your Mississippi Guard units are doing a great job. Morale seemed high, and they’re definitely making an impact on keeping DC safe.
My Democratic colleagues need to wake up and recognize the harm this ongoing Schumer Shutdown of DHS is doing to our national security and our men and women in uniform.

Alaskans should be aware that last night, two Russian TU-142 “Bear” bombers entered both the Alaska and Canadian ADIZ. They were intercepted by the professional men and women of the Alaska Air Force and shadowed by F-35s out of Eielson, AWACS, and tanker aircraft in northwest of Alaska as the Bears flew east over the Arctic Ocean parallel to the North Slope.

Our Canadian allies took the handoff as the aircraft crossed into the Canadian ADIZ. On their return, Alaska-based F-22s out of JBER again shadowed the Bears until they departed the ADIZ.

Right now, our country is undertaking important military missions in the Middle East. But it is important to remember that, on a regular basis, incursions by our adversaries are also taking place in our great state.

In the past week, I chaired two different hearings—an Anchorage Commerce Committee hearing on U.S. maritime investments in the Arctic, and a Senate Armed Services Committee hearing on military readiness with four-star leadership from across the services. In both hearings, I highlighted these increasingly aggressive moves in our waters and airspace.

During the Anchorage hearing, witnesses testified that these incursions are becoming the new normal, and that these operations are likely being signed off directly by the dictators of Russia and China—Putin and Xi Jinping.

The good news is that the Arctic is no longer viewed as a strategic backwater by the Pentagon. I have been working for more than ten years to drive that point home, and we are finally seeing action in response to that call.

Today, we are undertaking the most significant military buildup in infrastructure and capabilities in Alaska since World War II—literally billions of dollars flowing into our state, with more to come. These investments will ensure our ability to project power globally and defend American interests in the Arctic and the Indo-Pacific.

Each week, we share the stories of individuals from across our district—our Hometown Heroes—men and women whose lives reflect the character, strength, and spirit of the community we are proud to call home.

This week, we honor a man who quite literally helped build that community: David Schrenk, whom we sadly lost this week.

Just a few weeks ago, I had the privilege of celebrating Dave’s 90th birthday with him in Warminster. Surrounded by friends, family, and neighbors whose lives he had touched, it was a beautiful reminder of the kind of life Dave lived—one defined by humility, hard work, and a deep pride in doing things the right way.

Dave’s story was the kind that built America. He grew up with very little, went to work early, learned a trade, and through grit and determination built a remarkable life rooted in family, faith, and service.

A proud union bricklayer, Dave earned his journeyman’s card and worked on projects throughout Philadelphia and New York before putting down roots here in Bucks County. Over the decades that followed, he helped shape and build much of the community we know today—founding David J. Schrenk Masonry Co., and later, D.J.S. Custom Home Builders, where his craftsmanship and reputation for excellence became well known across the region.

Dave believed deeply in the dignity of honest work and the pride that comes from building something that lasts. His motto captured that spirit perfectly:“Always be proud to tell people this is my work.”

Across Bucks County, there are countless places where that pride quite literally lives on in the walls, homes, and communities he helped build.

But Dave’s legacy extended far beyond brick and stone. He believed deeply in investing in the next generation—supporting local charities, mentoring young people, and remaining devoted to his alma mater, Williamson College of the Trades, where he served for many years on the Board of Trustees and helped guide countless young men beginning their own journeys in the skilled trades.

Above all, Dave considered his greatest accomplishment in life to be raising his five daughters—Debbie, Donna, Darlene, Dawn, and Dana—and instilling in them the virtues he lived by every day: faith, integrity, diligence, excellence, and service.

Dave Schrenk represented the enduring spirit of the American story—where hard work, craftsmanship, and character come together to build not just homes, but stronger communities.

It was an honor to celebrate his 90th birthday with him—and an even greater honor to remember the legacy he leaves behind.

A builder, mentor, and proud craftsman. One of Bucks County’s truly legendary Hometown Heroes. May we continue to build—and live—in a way that would make him proud.

George Taylor immigrated to Pennsylvania and learned the trade of ironworks. He served as a justice of the peace, as a member of the provincial assembly, and as a judge of the county court. G000592.text:
Today, I voted against a War Powers Resolution that would have forced an immediate end of military operations in Iran. Here's the full statement I just sent to press: 

The president has not provided sufficient clarity for why this action was necessary at this exact moment. But servicemembers are actively engaged in hostilities, our allies are under attack and the Iranian regime is more desperate than ever to reassert its power. While I do not believe that an abrupt about-face is a good course of action given the reality on the ground, that should not be construed as my approval. While conflict requires that we remain flexible to shifting circumstances, at this time I would not support Congressional authorization or funding for sustained combat operations.

The president has so far acted within the authorities given to him by Congress through the War Powers Act of 1973. He has been briefing Congress, and he has 60 days to make his case for ongoing operations. This is not an illegal war — but it could become one. 

There are reasonable constraints Congress should impose. I urge my colleagues to join me in passing the Resolution I have introduced with Congressman Josh Gottheimer, which would cut the president’s authorized timeline for military action to 30 days and prohibit the deployment of ground troops outside the context of search-and-rescue or intelligence gathering. A month is plenty of time for the president to make his case to the American people — and for Congress to weigh in.

Under the Constitution, the separation of powers is clear: Congress has the power to declare war. The President, as Commander in Chief, has the power to command the military in a war that Congress has authorized. With respect to the war in Iran, authorization has neither been sought by the President nor granted by Congress.

The President cannot constitutionally wage war without congressional authorization unless the nation has been attacked, is under attack, or faces an imminent attack. None of those conditions is present here.

For too long, we have operated under a theory of presidential war powers so open-ended that it lacks anything resembling a limiting principle. The issue before us is not Democrat versus Republican, nor progressive versus conservative. It is Congress versus the President. It is Article I versus Article II. 

The Founders did not declare independence 250 years ago to replace one king with another. Nor did the Framers intend for the Commander in Chief to wield the unilateral war-making authority of an 18th-century English monarch.

The notion that a President can plunge the United States into a regional war in one of the most volatile places on earth—without even briefing Congress, much less securing its authorization—is irreconcilable with the text, structure, and history of the Constitution.  

Instead of playing second fiddle to an imperial presidency, Congress must reclaim its rightful place as the first branch of government—exactly as the Founders intended. We are Article I for a reason. It is time we start acting like it.

On Tuesday, I attended the congressional briefing on Iran that I, and many others, requested prior to this weekend's strikes.

Last week, when it appeared we might preemptively vote on the War Powers Resolution while the U.S. and Iran were in the middle of negotiations I said I would be a no vote because I believed that calling up the resolution at that time could undermine negotiations and telegraph to the Ayatollah that we weren’t applying maximum pressure and that he could delay a deal.

A lot has changed in a week. The military operations carried out this weekend were not limited strikes. The President of the United States has said it’s a war. The Secretary of War has said it’s a war.  We don’t have to try to wordsmith this for the American people. They know it’s a war.

The Iranian regime has oppressed its people and trampled on human rights for decades. No one will miss the Ayatollah, and I am happy that he is no longer able to reign terror on his country. His regime has inflicted rape, torture, and horror on those who stood against the Ayatollah and is responsible for the deaths of tens of thousands of Iranians including the over 30,000 people that were killed in response to last year's protests. It is clear that Iran should never have a nuclear weapon.

Regardless of how one feels about this war, or this President, Congress's constitutional role in any declaration of war is a completely separate issue. I have consistently held that Congressional authorities have been eroded under Republican and Democratic administrations and ceded by both parties when they control the trifecta of House, Senate, and Presidency. However, over the last year we have seen a ludicrous increase in the speed of Congress's abdication of authority to the Executive Branch. We must begin to claw back that prerogative. We must reestablish our Article I authority which grants Congress all legislative powers. For too long we have been happy to let our Presidents legislate through rulemaking - a dangerous precedent that I have consistently opposed regardless of who sits in the Oval Office.

I will be voting in favor of the Massie-Khanna War Powers Resolution.

The resolution that we will be voting on this week reclaims Congressional authority over the declaration of war. Additionally, it doesn’t prevent continued operations to protect our bases, assets, and personnel in Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Israel, Oman, Jordan, Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates, Iraq, and Kuwait – all of which are currently under attack by Iran – nor the continued sharing of intelligence with our allies.
 
Congress is on the verge of irrelevancy. We have done this to ourselves, and no one is coming to save us if we don’t show some sign of life.

I am also thinking of my constituents, the Levinson family, who I have represented since I served in the Florida State Legislature. Robert Levinson vanished in Iran in 2007 and for nearly 19 years, Iran has lied, obstructed, and refused to answer for his kidnapping, detention, and death. Robert’s loved ones deserve the truth of what happened to him in Iranian custody and to have his remains returned home.

Today, I voted against Rep. Massie’s War Powers Resolution regarding hostilities with Iran. When voting my duty is to uphold the Constitution and the precedent set by our Founders. 

In 1801, President Thomas Jefferson, Secretary of State James Madison, and Treasury Secretary Albert Gallatin deliberated on whether the United States could launch a defensive attack against the Islamic North African Barbary pirates without a declaration of war from Congress. At that time, the Barbary pirates were threatening the safety and security of Americans, much like the radical Iranian regime is doing today. 

During these deliberations, our Founders came to the determination that while “The executive cannot put us in a state of war…if we be put into that state either by the declaration of Congress or of the other nation, the command & direction of the public force then belongs to the Executive.” Following the Founders’ interpretation of the Constitution and precedent, it is key to understand that we are taking defensive actions rather than launching an offensive attack. 

As President Thomas Jefferson stated when dealing with the Barbary pirates, “Unauthorized by the Constitution, without the sanction of Congress, to go beyond the line of defense, the vessel being disabled from committing further hostilities, was liberated with its crew. The legislature will doubtless consider whether, by authorising measures of offense also, they will place our force on an equal footing with that of its adversaries.” 

This comment by Jefferson means that there is a fine line that must be walked between taking an offensive and defensive posture. According to the decision made by Jefferson and Father of our Constitution, James Madison, the Executive has the right to launch defensive attacks against actively hostile nations until they are neutralized from committing further hostilities. 

“Death to America” was not merely an empty threat, it this was a key part of the Ayatollah's radical political extremism which is laid out in the Qaran. They have been declaring war on us, in intervals for the last 47 years. Between 2003-2011 Iranian proxies killed over 600 American troops. In 2020, Iran launched a dozen ballistic missiles at a US air base, injuring over 100 American servicemembers. Just recently, intelligence showed that Iran was mere months away from developing missile and nuclear capabilities that would have overwhelmed our interception capabilities, limiting the ability of the United States to protect itself. 

A nuclear-armed Iran is simply unacceptable. This heightened security risk, in tandem with Iran’s historical attacks against Americans and their status as the largest state sponsor of terrorism in the world, necessitated defensive US military action to protect our nation and our people until they are “disabled from committing further hostilities.”

Yesterday, I voted to refer Rep. Nancy Mace’s resolution, H. Res. 1100, to the House Ethics Committee. While I firmly believe that those who have violated the House’s Code of Official Conduct ought to be duly punished, this legislation, as written, is flawed. 

Not only did the House Ethics Committee state that the resolution would discourage witness participation, it also laid the groundwork for punishing ALLEGED misconduct versus allowing fact to determine guilt.

True justice requires that we do not treat alleged misconduct as proof of guilt. This concept is found throughout the Bible (including in Deuteronomy 19:15, Matthew 18:16, and 2 Corinthians 13:1), which states that “every fact is to be confirmed be the testimony of two or three witnesses.”

It is no wonder, then, that common law shares this principle and that our Biblically literate Founders incorporated this concept into our Constitution, such as when they required that two or more witnesses were necessary for determining guilt in cases of treason (Article III, Section 3, Clause 1).

Today, I join the nation in mourning the passing of Dr. Norman C. Francis. For generations of Louisianans, and for people across this country, he represented what steady, faithful leadership in education truly looks like.
 
During his nearly five decades leading Xavier University of Louisiana, Dr. Francis helped transform the institution into a national model of academic excellence and opportunity, especially for students pursuing careers in medicine, science, and public service. His leadership opened doors for countless young people and strengthened the legacy of historically black colleges and universities across our nation. 
 
What made Dr. Francis so remarkable was not only his accomplishments, but his quiet strength, humility, and his belief in the power of education to change lives. Louisiana has lost a historic force for education and opportunity, but the impact of Dr. Francis’ life and work will continue to be felt for generations to come.
 
Dr. Francis’ lifetime of leadership will continue to shape Xavier University, our state, and the future of higher education. My thoughts and prayers are with the Francis family and everyone whose lives were touched by Dr. Francis.

This morning, we lost a giant in the fight for civil rights, justice, and equality. More than that, we lost a man of deep faith and conviction whose life helped bend the arc of this nation toward justice.

As a young person, I had the honor of supporting Reverend Jackson’s historic presidential campaign and witnessed firsthand the faith, courage, and moral clarity that defined his leadership. Over the years, I came to know not only the power of his public voice, but the strength of his personal example. His influence helped shape my own commitment to service and the ongoing work of a more just nation.

I am deeply grateful for his legacy that is not only written in history books, but living on in the people he shaped and the work that we are all blessed to continue because he chose to serve.

My thoughts and prayers are with the entire Jackson family, and all those who are grieving this profound loss today. The greatest way we can honor Reverend Jackson is by carrying forward his historic impact through the continued work for justice and equality for all.

WORLD_FRANCE_PRESIDENT.text:
Je me suis entretenu avec le Président syrien Ahmad Al-Charaa ainsi que le Président libanais Joseph Aoun.
                                                                      
La France œuvre avec ses partenaires à éviter que le conflit ne se propage davantage dans la région.

La souveraineté et l’intégrité territoriale de la Syrie et du Liban, comme de chaque pays dans la région, doivent être respectées. 

Les déstabilisations en cours ne peuvent laisser aucune place au terrorisme. La France y veillera.

Alors que la Force des Nations unies au Liban joue un rôle clé de stabilisation au sud du Liban, je condamne fermement l’attaque inacceptable qui a frappé aujourd’hui des membres de son contingent. La France y restera engagée.

أجريتُ محادثات مع الرئيس السوري احمد  الشرع، وكذلك مع الرئيس اللبناني جوزيف عون.
             
تعمل فرنسا مع شركائها على الحيلولة دون اتساع رقعة النزاع أكثر في المنطقة.

يجب احترام سيادة سوريا ولبنان وسلامتهما الإقليمية، كما يجب احترام سيادة كل بلد في المنطقة وسلامته الإقليمية.

إن أعمال زعزعة الاستقرار الجارية لا يجوز أن تترك أي مجال للإرهاب. وستسهر فرنسا على ذلك.

وفي وقت تؤدي فيه قوة الأمم المتحدة في لبنان دورًا أساسيًا في تحقيق الاستقرار في جنوب لبنان، فإنني أدين بشدة الهجوم غير المقبول الذي استهدف اليوم أفرادًا من وحدتها. وستظل فرنسا ملتزمة هناك.

تحدثتُ للتو مع رئيس الوزراء العراقي محمد شياع السوداني.
                                                         
وأعربتُ له عن تضامن فرنسا الكامل مع العراق في مواجهة التصعيد الجاري في الشرق الادنى و الشرق الأوسط. وجددتُ دعمي لجهوده الحازمة من أجل عدم جرّ العراق إلى هذا النزاع.

إن استقرار البلاد أمرٌ أساسي للمنطقة بأسرها. وتدعم فرنسا الاحترام الكامل لسيادة العراق وأمنه ووحدة أراضيه.

Je lui ai exprimé la pleine solidarité de la France avec l’Irak face à l’escalade en cours au Proche et au Moyen-Orient. J'ai renouvelé mon appui à son action résolue pour que l'Irak ne soit pas entraîné dans le conflit.

La stabilité du pays est essentielle pour toute la région. La France soutient le plein respect de la souveraineté, de la sécurité, et de l’intégrité territoriale de l’Irak.
